paper_metadata.title: SWE-Stream: Scaling Executable Training Data for SWE Agents via Progressive Construction and Elastic Streaming
paper_metadata.abstract: Software engineering agents have advanced rapidly, but scaling their training remains constrained by the limited availability of high-quality executable tasks. Development histories contain valuable signals for constructing such tasks, yet they often require substantial reconstruction due to incomplete environments, missing tests, and inconsistent artifacts. We present SWE-Stream, a system for scaling executable SWE training data through progressive construction and elastic streaming execution. SWE-Stream progressively validates and refines task candidates, reusing existing artifacts when possible and applying targeted completion only when necessary. An elastic scheduler asynchronously coordinates construction stages under shared resource constraints, adapting execution budgets based on observed workload demands. Using development histories from 10,728 repositories across six programming languages, SWE-Stream constructs 80,874 validated tasks and collects 118,688 successful trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 on these trajectories achieves resolve rates of 69.0%, 49.3%, and 45.42% on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, respectively. In a controlled comparison with approximately matched training budgets, SWE-Stream achieves a 45.6% resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming three existing data sources. Moreover, its streaming construction strategy improves efficiency, delivering $1.45\times$ the accepted-task throughput of batch construction and accepting 13.2% more tasks than fixed-limit streaming.

21: Every episode records tokens, turn timings, and a timestamped timeline of rollout and training. Those records are what the simulator is checked against. Setup and the launch script are in [TRAINING.md](TRAINING.md). What each logged number means is in [METRICS.md](METRICS.md).

25: `src/simulator` is a trace-driven discrete-event simulator of one GRPO step. A trace says what work there was. An adapter turns it into an IR of sessions, requests, tool tasks, and resource leases. A config bundle says what system runs that work: SGLang replicas, tensor-parallel size, KV cache, concurrency caps, container and eval slots, and a cost model fitted on a measured grid. The engine then runs the work on that system.

27: The scheduler is SGLang's own scheduler, with the model worker stubbed out. Each forward is priced by the cost model. Container starts, tool calls, and grading take their durations from the trace, or from priors when the trace did not record them. The clock follows SGLang's overlap schedule: a request's arrival is when the previous turn finished generating plus the tool time from the trace, not a timestamp copied out of a previous run.

The harness covers per-task Docker sandboxes, full JSONL trajectories with a replay viewer, a failure taxonomy, reward-hacking detection and paired ablation statistics.

47: - **Planning:** the task prompt asks the model to restate the issue and plan its search.
49: - **Self-verification gate:** `submit` is rejected once if no tests have run since the last edit. It only rejects once, so the agent can never deadlock.

53: Each iteration makes one model call and runs every tool call in that response. The loop continues while the model keeps calling tools. Every episode ends with exactly one of these causes, which is logged:
57: | `submit` | The model called `submit` and the scaffold accepted it. |
58: | `end_turn_no_submit` | The model stopped calling tools, was nudged once, and stopped again. |
63: | `refusal` | The model declined (`stop_reason: refusal`). |
69: - **Premature success** (submitting an untested change). Caught by the verification gate.

74: Current Claude models sign their thinking blocks over the conversation that comes before them, and the API rejects a request that replays those blocks after earlier history was edited. So this agent never trims or masks old tool outputs in place.

76: When the prompt passes the token budget, or the model reports `model_context_window_exceeded`, the conversation is **reset**. A fresh conversation starts with the original task plus a deterministic state summary that the harness tracks itself:
83: The summary costs no extra model call. Resets are capped and logged. See [`agent/context.py`](agent/context.py).

90: - **Pinned configuration.** The run fingerprint covers the model ID, thinking mode, effort level, budgets and pricing. Every prompt template is a checked-in file whose SHA-256 is logged in each trajectory. The exact model string the API reports is logged for every call. A run refuses to resume if its config changed.

91: - **Sampling is not seedable.** Current models reject non-default `temperature`/`top_p`/`top_k`, so runs are not bit-for-bit reproducible. Instead, behaviour is pinned through `thinking` and `effort`, and **run-to-run variance should be measured** by repeating the same subset (see [Repeats](#repeats-and-variance)). The seed controls which tasks go into the subset.

92: - **Isolation.** Each task gets its own container from the official per-instance image, with `--network none` and memory/CPU limits. The container is destroyed afterwards. Grading happens in a separate fresh container run by the official harness.

candidate.title: From Conceptual EneMonIE to an Executable Backend: A Modular Architecture for Energy Information Extractionand Grounded Question Answering

paper_metadata.title: From Conceptual EneMonIE to an Executable Backend: A Modular Architecture for Energy Information Extractionand Grounded Question Answering
paper_metadata.abstract: The original EneMonIE proposal describes a Web-based semantic system for continuously monitoring energy trends through targeted information extraction from heterogeneous online media. This article presents EneMonIE-Backend, an implementation-derived redesign that converts that conceptual pipeline into a modular, executable, and application-independent backend. The architecture separates five concerns: data sources, acquisition and normalization, semantic processing, knowledge organization, and persistent storage. It operationalizes configurable connectors for RSS feeds, URL collections, arXiv, social-media JSON files, and open-data CSV files; it also introduces question-driven Web search and scraping. Relevant documents pass through energy categorization, named entity recognition, temporal and event extraction, source sensitive sentiment analysis, and extractive summarization. The resulting semantic representations support entity co-occurrence graphs, cross-document interlinking, cluster-level information fusion, and relational persistence in SQLite. Three grounded question-answering paths are exposed at the backend level: live Web evidence, the stored corpus, and selected configured resources. Answer generation uses a language model when configured and otherwise falls back to deterministic extractive output. Unlike the original proposal, the presented architecture deliberately excludes the user-interface and server-side application layers, allowing the semantic core to be embedded in different applications. A deterministic smoke validation confirms relevance filtering, persistence, clustering, evidence retrieval, and document deletion. The work provides a reproducible architectural basis for future evaluation on larger multilingual energy corpora.

candidate.title: Continually Post-training Small Models via Synthetic Self-distillation

review_pool.abstract_primary: Continual post-training faces a dual challenge of acquisition and retention: models must learn new capabilities while preserving prior knowledge. While Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) mitigates this using self-supervision with in-context demonstrations, it relies on strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities. Consequently, SDFT fails on smaller models critical for low-latency, on-device use. To enable continual learning at smaller scales, we first identify the root cause of failure. We show that poor acquisition and forgetting correlate linearly with the post-trained model's distribution shift, revealing the necessity of in-distribution learning. We thus introduce Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), imitating SDFT's in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger, same-family aligner. Coupled with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, this provides the high-quality supervision small models require without breaking their original distribution. Evaluations spanning 4 acquisition datasets (including a mixture) and 14 retention benchmarks show SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 methods (including off- and on-policy distillation) across 3 small model scales. Extensive further analyses confirm SynthSelf paves the way toward effective small-model continual learning.

candidate.title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization

review_pool.publication_date_basis: arXiv citation_date metadata; null/unknown when absent
review_pool.abstract_primary: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this \emph{KV concentration} and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose \emph{KV4-RL}, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves $1.80\times$ cumulative rollout speedup and $1.27\times$ cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching $1.97\times$ rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.
